1. Orf (parapoxvirus — contagious ecthyma) — single nodular papulonodule on hand after handling infected animals; often painless or mildly tender and without systemic symptoms. (Next steps: close-up photo; lesion swab for parapox/orthopox PCR if available; clinical follow-up — usually self-limited.)
2. Tularemia (ulceroglandular Francisella tularensis) — classic exposure from hares/rabbits; may present as a hand ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy and can be systemic (fever may be absent early). (Next: focused exam for ulcer/eschar and ipsilateral lymph nodes; F. tularensis PCR/serology; CBC/CRP; consider early empiric therapy if suspicion high.)
3. Herpetic whitlow (HSV infection of the finger) — painful vesicular lesions on hand/finger; may be confused with other pustular lesions. (Next: HSV PCR/swab of lesion, or viral culture; ask specifically about prior cold sores.)
4. Bacterial skin infection (Staphylococcus/streptococcal pustule, abscess, or cellulitis) — common cause of hand lesions; may produce pus, erythema, tenderness. (Next: wound culture and Gram stain if drainage; consider empirical anti-staphylococcal antibiotics if purulence/cellulitis.)
5. Cutaneous anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) — less likely but important to consider with animal contact; typically a painless black eschar with marked surrounding edema. (Next: inspect for painless eschar/edema; Gram stain/culture/PCR for B. anthracis and urgent treatment if suspected.)

Recommended immediate actions (to narrow diagnosis): provide a clear close-up photo of the lesion, allow physical exam of the affected hand (look for ulcer/eschar, vesicles, tenderness, regional lymphadenopathy, edema), and obtain lesion swabs for: bacterial culture/Gram stain, HSV PCR, and — given rabbit exposure — F. tularensis PCR/serology (and parapox PCR if available).
